title: Rosemarys Baby

jokes.text: The GE Followship Award — presented annually to the person who best exemplifies a follower
jokes.setup: Jack announces an award with great fanfare, calling it a 'fellowship' award
jokes.punchline: It's actually a 'followship' award — celebrating being a compliant corporate follower, which is a thinly veiled dig at Liz for caving to GE's demands
jokes.explanation: Sharp corporate satire with excellent setup — the mispronunciation/wordplay of fellowship→followship is clever and loaded with thematic meaning. Jack's sincerity in the delivery makes the contempt for Liz funnier. Strong character work for both Jack and Liz.

jokes.text: Liz immediately protests 'I'm not a follower' — then hears it comes with ten grand and immediately says 'I accept this proudly on behalf of followers everywhere'
jokes.setup: Liz objects to being called a follower
jokes.punchline: The instant she hears it comes with $10,000 she reverses completely, with maximum self-satisfied dignity
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character integration — this is quintessential Liz Lemon. The beat between protest and capitulation is perfectly timed. The grandiose 'on behalf of followers everywhere' is the right amount of self-delusion. This defines her arc for the episode in two sentences.

jokes.text: Jack uses the word 'adverlingus' to describe product integration
jokes.setup: Jack lists corporate buzzwords: product integration, cross-promotion...
jokes.punchline: 'adverlingus' — a portmanteau of 'advertising' and 'cunnilingus,' implying corporate content is an act of corporate oral sex on the audience
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best wordplay jokes. 'Adverlingus' is a genuinely brilliant coinage — perfectly describes the nature of advertiser-friendly content with maximum shock-economy. Delivered by Jack as a straight corporate term makes it even better. Highly quotable and original.

jokes.text: He has a microwave for a head! But it's such an excellent GE microwave.
jokes.setup: Liz complains about having to do a sketch where a character literally has a microwave for a head
jokes.punchline: Jack's defense is not that it's artistically valid — only that it's an excellent GE microwave
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of the premise (microwave head) is funny on its own, but Jack's pivot to brand quality is the real joke — it perfectly encapsulates corporate logic. Good economy, strong character voice for Jack.

jokes.text: Where do you invest your money, Liz? / I have, like, 12 grand in checking. / Are you an immigrant?
jokes.setup: Jack mocks the idea of a 401K, then asks where Liz invests
jokes.punchline: Liz reveals she keeps $12,000 in checking like a child; Jack's response 'Are you an immigrant?' is a perfect class-gap punchline
jokes.explanation: The comedic gap between Jack's patrician financial world and Liz's complete financial cluelessness is a rich vein for the show. 'Are you an immigrant?' lands hard because it's both insulting and weirdly accurate as a class signifier. Strong Liz/Jack dynamic.

jokes.text: If I can't be Monique fat, I have to be Teri Hatcher thin. Either way, you're laughin'.
jokes.setup: Someone compliments Ms. Moroney on losing weight quickly
jokes.punchline: She frames celebrity body image as a binary: either you're famously overweight or famously skeletal — both are winning strategies
jokes.explanation: Sharp celebrity/body image satire delivered with breezy confidence. The specific name-drops (Monique, Teri Hatcher) are well-chosen contrasts. 'Either way, you're laughin'' has a great throwaway quality. Slightly docked for character integration — this could work in other characters' mouths.

jokes.text: Donnie spills something on Ms. Moroney's uniform and attempts to wipe it off, then splashes water on her — followed by screaming
jokes.setup: Donnie tries to clean the stain, asking her to turn around
jokes.punchline: The 'cleaning' escalates to an apparent burning/scalding (the scream), making it comically worse — a classic slapstick escalation
jokes.explanation: Standard physical escalation gag — the attempt to fix a problem makes it worse. Functional but not particularly original. Sets up the page jacket subplot. The scream/burn is inferred and doesn't add much comedically beyond the setup.

jokes.text: Is she one of the ladies who tried to shoot Gerald Ford?
jokes.setup: Someone asks if Liz knows who Rosemary Howard is, a famous comedy writer
jokes.punchline: Liz guesses she's one of the women who attempted to assassinate Gerald Ford — a hilariously specific wrong answer
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it's so specifically wrong — not 'a historical figure' but precisely the women who tried to shoot Gerald Ford. The absurd specificity is the joke. Good economy and solid misdirection structure.

jokes.text: Pardon me! / Pardon you? You were already pardoned! / It's funny 'cause it's true.
jokes.setup: Liz excuses herself with 'pardon me' and Rosemary responds as if it's a political pardon reference
jokes.punchline: 'You were already pardoned!' — referencing Gerald Ford's pardon of Nixon, then immediately commenting 'It's funny 'cause it's true' — meta-commentary on its own joke
jokes.explanation: A clever double-layered joke: wordplay on 'pardon' that pays off a setup from the Gerald Ford reference just moments earlier, AND immediately commented on with meta-awareness. The 'it's funny 'cause it's true' is the kind of self-satisfied comedian behavior that also characterizes Rosemary. Tight construction.

jokes.text: I used to make my friends act out your skits the next day. When I say friends, I mean my Fisher Price... my friend dolls. Because I didn't have a lot of friends.
jokes.setup: Liz describes acting out Rosemary's skits with friends
jokes.punchline: Catches herself mid-sentence — 'Fisher Price' implies toys, she walks it back to 'friend dolls,' then admits she had no friends. The correction makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: Pure Liz Lemon — the self-correction that digs her deeper is a signature comedic move for the character. The stammer, the euphemism 'friend dolls,' and the defeated admission all land. Strong character integration — this only works for a character with Liz's established social awkwardness.

jokes.text: Oh, boy. Am I still talking? / You're gonna kill me, aren't you?
jokes.setup: Liz continues babbling excitedly at her idol
jokes.punchline: Rosemary's deadpan 'You're gonna kill me, aren't you?' — treating Liz's enthusiasm as a threat
jokes.explanation: Good comedic beat — Rosemary's deadpan response reframes Liz's fangirl enthusiasm as menacing. Works well as character introduction for Rosemary's dry wit. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I grew up wanting to be Samantha Stevens on Bewitched. Closest I got was being married to a gay guy for two years.
jokes.setup: Liz says she grew up wanting to be Rosemary; Rosemary responds with her own aspirational figure
jokes.punchline: Her life approximation of Samantha Stevens — a magical woman with an adoring husband — was marrying a closeted gay man
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured self-deprecating joke. The setup creates expectation of something aspirational; the punchline is a lateral slide into a very specific personal disaster. Economy is excellent — it sketches Rosemary's character instantly. The Bewitched connection (magical → gay husband) is a deft comic logic leap.

jokes.text: You are my heroine. And by heroine, I mean lady hero. I don't wanna inject you and listen to jazz.
jokes.setup: Liz calls Rosemary her 'heroine'
jokes.punchline: Immediately clarifies the drug meaning, then paints a specific and absurd alternative image: injecting Rosemary and listening to jazz
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The wordplay on heroine/heroin is familiar, but the specific extension — 'inject you and listen to jazz' — is what elevates it. The jazz detail is precise and funny. Liz's earnest over-explanation is perfectly in-character. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Who would have ever known there was so many words? It was like a Mos Def CD.
jokes.setup: Tracy apparently desecrated something — implied he attempted to sing/perform the national anthem and mangled it badly
jokes.punchline: His defense/explanation: didn't know there were so many words — comparing it to a Mos Def CD (implying overwhelming lyrical density)
jokes.explanation: The Tracy Jordan logic is strong here — his bafflement at lyrical density is funny. The Mos Def comparison is a good non-sequitur that works as character comedy (Tracy's frame of reference is entirely celebrity/entertainment). Good Tracy voice.

jokes.text: You go forth and be crazy... except no dog fighting, okay? That seems to be the one thing that's off limits these days.
jokes.setup: Jack tells Tracy stars can do whatever they want
jokes.punchline: He carves out only one exception — dog fighting — with the breezy qualifier 'that seems to be the one thing that's off limits these days,' implying everything else (however awful) is fine
jokes.explanation: The 'these days' qualifier is the key — it implies dog fighting used to be acceptable celebrity behavior, which is a dark satirical jab at celebrity culture and its shifting moral goalposts. Jack's breezy delivery of something horrifying is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: We gotta start doing dog fights. I know it's repulsive and hideous. But it's the only thing Jack Donaghy told me I cannot do. So I gotta do it!
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks Tracy what's on his mind
jokes.punchline: Tracy's entire motivation for dog fighting is explicitly that Jack said not to — he acknowledges it's horrible but the prohibition is the only reason he needs
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tracy Jordan character work — the joke is that Tracy has no other motivation beyond defiance of authority, not even interest in the activity itself. This sets up the whole Tracy subplot with perfect character logic. The self-awareness ('I know it's repulsive') makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Dog fighting it is. Make it happen.
jokes.setup: Kenneth passionately protests against dog fighting as the most disgusting vile thing
jokes.punchline: Tracy's completely flat, corporate-boss-style 'Dog fighting it is. Make it happen.' — treating Kenneth's moral outrage as a pitch approval
jokes.explanation: The economy here is nearly perfect — Tracy adopts Jack's corporate register ('make it happen') to greenlight something horrifying. The contrast between Kenneth's moral passion and Tracy's boardroom dismissal is the whole joke. Very punchy delivery implied.

jokes.text: Man, this is Phil Spector's entourage all over again. And his foot lingered.
jokes.setup: Rosemary and Liz are sharing backstage stories
jokes.punchline: Phil Spector's entourage story ends with the unsettling detail 'and his foot lingered' — unexplained but clearly horrible
jokes.explanation: The joke functions on the dark comedy of unexplained celebrity creepiness — Phil Spector was known for bizarre/violent behavior, and the foot detail is both specific enough to be funny and vague enough to be disturbing. Good economy, strong dark tone.

jokes.text: I'll never watch Happy Days the same way again.
jokes.setup: Rosemary's story about Phil Spector's entourage is apparently disturbing
jokes.punchline: Liz's reaction implicates Happy Days in whatever horrible thing happened — a darkly funny non-sequitur that implies a Happy Days connection to the story
jokes.explanation: The joke leaves the Happy Days connection completely unexplained, which is funnier than any explanation would be. The specificity of naming Happy Days makes it land. Good dark comedy economy.

jokes.text: I miss live TV. It's like sex, you know? It's almost better when everything goes horribly wrong.
jokes.setup: Rosemary is waxing nostalgic about live television
jokes.punchline: The sex comparison — specifically that it's 'almost better when everything goes horribly wrong' — is the comedic truth that lands
jokes.explanation: The sex/live TV comparison is a classic analogy joke, but the twist — 'better when everything goes horribly wrong' — is the sharp, honest detail that makes it work. Good delivery vehicle for Rosemary's character as a freewheeling veteran.

jokes.text: Does everyone still do blow in Joe Garagiola's office? Which one is blow again? Is that cocaine?
jokes.setup: Rosemary asks about NBC's drug culture with insider familiarity
jokes.punchline: Liz's innocent 'Which one is blow again? Is that cocaine?' — revealing she's so square she doesn't even know drug slang
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke: Rosemary casually namedrops Joe Garagiola and cocaine culture as if asking about the weather (great character establishment), and Liz's response reveals she's too nerdy/square to know basic drug terminology. The contrast between the two women's worldliness is perfectly done.

jokes.text: This is a prop from the classic NBC series Supercomputer. 1975 to 1975.
jokes.setup: Ms. Moroney enters what appears to be a tech setup — Donnie is behind a prop computer
jokes.punchline: '1975 to 1975' — the show ran for less than a year, possibly a single season or even a single airing, delivered with the same pride as a long-running classic
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in the repetition of the same year — '1975 to 1975' — delivered straight. Perfect economy, absurdist in the best 30 Rock tradition. The 'classic' label applied to a show that clearly lasted one year or less is the irony. Rewatch bonus for catching the dates.

jokes.text: Mr. Perfect, Mr. Jesus loves me Parcell finally messed up? Do you know how long I've been waiting to transfer that thumbhead to CNBC in Paramus, New Jersey?
jokes.setup: Donnie discovers Kenneth made an error
jokes.punchline: His gleeful anticipation of sending Kenneth to CNBC in Paramus, New Jersey — the specificity of Paramus as the ultimate punishment destination is funny
jokes.explanation: 'Thumbhead' is a funny insult, and Paramus NJ as a destination of professional exile is a very specific, locally-resonant joke. The depth of Donnie's grudge against Kenneth is funny. 'Mr. Jesus loves me Parcell' is a good character tag.

jokes.text: You've probably never seen breasts before. So I'm gonna lean over this desk and you're gonna give me a new page jacket.
jokes.setup: Donnie wants something from Kenneth and tries to leverage what she assumes is his weakness
jokes.punchline: She assumes the wholesome Kenneth has never seen breasts and attempts to use this as blackmail
jokes.explanation: Sets up a good subversion — the assumption about Kenneth's innocence is reasonable given his character, which makes the comeback land well. Slightly cringe-y in premise but within the show's register.

jokes.text: Please. I breast fed 'til I was 11. So I've forgotten more about a woman's chest than you'll ever know.
jokes.setup: Donnie tries to seduce Kenneth with the promise of seeing her breasts
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's completely sincere, rural-America response: he was breastfed until age 11, framed as proof of sophistication
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Kenneth's response works on multiple levels: it's a total reversal of the expected reaction, the detail (breastfed until 11) suggests a deeply weird rural upbringing, the delivery 'I've forgotten more about a woman's chest than you'll ever know' is absurdly confident, and it's completely in character — Kenneth's naïve but weirdly experienced in inexplicable ways. Near-perfect character integration, high originality, excellent structure. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: But... I'm on TV. / I said, 'Good day.' / No, you didn't. / Well, I meant to. / Kenneth Parcell is finished. Finished!
jokes.setup: Donnie's gambit fails; she tries to recover with a dismissive 'Good day'
jokes.punchline: Kenneth points out she didn't actually say it; Donnie admits 'I meant to' then overcompensates with melodramatic 'Kenneth Parcell is FINISHED!'
jokes.explanation: The 'I meant to' admission is a funny deflation of Donnie's pomposity, and the pivot to theatrical villain mode ('FINISHED!') is a good escalation. The 'I'm on TV' excuse for attempted sexual bribery is also a nice dark touch.

jokes.text: We open on a New Orleans abortion clinic. A beautiful mulatto... / Uh, I don't think we're allowed to use any of those words.
jokes.setup: Writers' room pitching sketch ideas; Rosemary enthusiastically pitches
jokes.punchline: A writer immediately shuts her down — all the words in the pitch are off-limits before she even gets to the sketch
jokes.explanation: A sharp joke about how comedy standards have changed — Rosemary's old-school pitch hits every modern taboo in the first sentence. The speed of the shutdown is the joke: she barely starts before it's already unsalvageable. Good satirical commentary on generational comedy gaps.

jokes.text: Don't you get it? The mailbox was Haldeman. / Is that a person who lived?
jokes.setup: Rosemary passionately explains the political subtext of the mailbox sketch
jokes.punchline: The young writer asks 'Is that a person who lived?' — Haldeman being Nixon's chief of staff, completely unknown to the younger generation
jokes.explanation: The punchline captures the generational knowledge gap perfectly. 'Is that a person who lived?' is a fantastic deflating line — it's not even hostile, just genuinely ignorant, which is funnier. Also ties back to the Gerald Ford/pardon joke earlier.

jokes.text: We get Josh in blackface, right? And then we get Tracy to call him a—!
jokes.setup: Rosemary pitches a race-relations sketch with escalating inappropriateness
jokes.punchline: The sketch idea — a white man in blackface being called a slur by a Black man — is presented with absolute enthusiasm as edgy television
jokes.explanation: Works as satire of old-school TV's problematic 'edginess' — the joke is on Rosemary's certainty that this is genius television. The reaction from the room is implied to be horror. Slightly weaker than the surrounding jokes because the target (racist-edgy-TV) is obvious.

jokes.text: I'd watch that.
jokes.setup: The writers are all appalled by Rosemary's blackface pitch
jokes.punchline: Tracy's flat, genuine 'I'd watch that' — as the person who would be doing the calling, his approval is simultaneously the funniest and most disturbing response
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum impact. Tracy's complete sincerity combined with his unique position (as the Black man who would be saying the slur) makes 'I'd watch that' land as both a character-perfect reaction and a sharp satirical commentary. Perfect economy. Among the episode's best.

jokes.text: You can't do race stuff on TV. It's too sensitive. / We would have done that on the Mandrell Sisters!
jokes.setup: Liz explains modern TV constraints
jokes.punchline: Rosemary invokes the Mandrell Sisters as a beacon of bold programming — a show not remembered for racial boundary-pushing at all
jokes.explanation: The humor is in Rosemary's misremembering of TV history — the Mandrell Sisters was a wholesome country music variety show, not known for racial politics. This deepens the joke that Rosemary's memory of her era's bravery may be significantly inflated.

jokes.text: Liz says 'I'm not some... follower' with visible self-consciousness
jokes.setup: Rosemary tells Liz she's not a cog in the machine
jokes.punchline: Liz uses the exact word from her opening award — 'follower' — catching herself with a beat, showing she's aware of the irony
jokes.explanation: A structurally satisfying callback that also functions as character insight — Liz's pause before 'follower' shows she knows exactly what she won that morning. The rewatch bonus applies because the full weight of the callback requires remembering the opening.

jokes.text: Barry the humping dog is shopping for a GE washer and dryer. / Have not seen that before. / Sharp idea.
jokes.setup: Writers' room pitches; Frank offers 'Barry the humping dog' looking at GE appliances
jokes.punchline: Jack's 'Have not seen that before. Sharp idea.' — delivered as sincere approval despite the sketch being painfully obvious product integration
jokes.explanation: A callback to the product integration theme of the episode. Jack's deadpan endorsement of the most transparently awful creative idea is a solid piece of satire. The 'Barry the humping dog' pitch is also funny as a symbol of what the show has sunk to.

jokes.text: What? No! You idiots! I built a dog fighting pit in my basement for this?
jokes.setup: Tracy says he has dogs outside, implying a dog fight is about to happen
jokes.punchline: The dogs are brought in and are clearly just pet dogs — Tracy has built an actual fighting pit in his basement for what turns out to be totally innocent dogs
jokes.explanation: The twist (Tracy actually built a basement pit) retroactively makes his earlier enthusiasm funnier — he committed fully to the bit. The misdirection works well because the audience expected a punchline about Tracy not actually doing it; instead he went further than expected in the wrong direction.

jokes.text: Hey, props gave me a bunch of dog penises for you to look at. / Oh, great, thanks.
jokes.setup: A page delivers something to Liz in the hallway
jokes.punchline: The casual delivery and acceptance of a bag of dog penises as a normal work task — Liz's 'Oh, great, thanks' is the absurdist straight-man response
jokes.explanation: A callback to the dog penis sketch that lands because of how casually it's delivered. The joke is in the normalcy — this is just another Tuesday at TGS. Excellent economy. The callback works even without remembering the sketch setup.

jokes.text: Fire her. And don't ever make me talk to a woman that old again.
jokes.setup: Rosemary has just charmed Jack with her ideas; Liz thinks it went well
jokes.punchline: Jack's immediate verdict — fire her — plus the rider about not wanting to talk to old women again, delivered with corporate efficiency
jokes.explanation: The misdirection (Rosemary thought she was charming him) plus Jack's absolute ruthlessness — with the additional ageism added as a rider as if it's a business condition — is sharp character work. Very Jack Donaghy.

jokes.text: Yes, you can. It's easy. Observe. Jonathan, you're fired! / What? No! God, no! No, I won't fire her.
jokes.setup: Liz says she can't fire Rosemary; Jack says it's easy
jokes.punchline: Jack demonstrates on Jonathan — his assistant — who reacts with genuine anguish before Jack clarifies it was just a demonstration
jokes.explanation: Jonathan's disproportionate devastation at 'you're fired' — 'What? No! God, no!' — reveals the depth of his Jack-dependency in a single beat. The gag works because Jack's complete indifference to the collateral damage of his demonstration is so in-character.

jokes.text: You're like the talking mailbox. / I'm gonna assume that's a Haldeman reference. In which case, I thank you.
jokes.setup: Liz insults Jack by calling him 'the talking mailbox'
jokes.punchline: Jack reframes the insult as a Watergate-era political allegory complimenting him — choosing to interpret it as flattering rather than insulting
jokes.explanation: The callback to the mailbox-as-Haldeman joke works because Jack immediately adopts the political subtext as his own — he'd rather be a powerful Nixon aide than the butt of a simpler insult. Strong character integration for Jack's ego.

jokes.text: You are a suit. You feed off the creativity and hard work of other people and turn it into commercials and pie charts and triangle graphs.
jokes.setup: Liz is on a passionate anti-corporate rant
jokes.punchline: 'Triangle graphs' — not a real thing, which she immediately admits
jokes.explanation: The rant is standard but 'triangle graphs' is the payoff — the invented corporate jargon that immediately deflates Liz's passion. The self-undercut ('I don't know! It sounded real.') is perfect Liz Lemon.

jokes.text: No, this is my show. And once a week I rent it out to the good people at the erectile dysfunction companies.
jokes.setup: Liz claims 'this is my show'
jokes.punchline: Jack agrees it's his show — but with the matter-of-fact caveat that it's rented weekly to erectile dysfunction advertisers
jokes.explanation: Another sharp piece of corporate/TV satire. The 'erectile dysfunction companies' specificity is funny — not 'advertisers' but specifically the ED advertisers that saturate late-night TV. Jack's cheerful matter-of-factness about this arrangement is great character work.

jokes.text: Suck it up, nerd.
jokes.setup: Liz makes her impassioned final stand, threatening to quit if Rosemary is fired
jokes.punchline: Jack's response to her entire speech: three words, maximum dismissiveness
jokes.explanation: 'Suck it up, nerd' is a masterclass in comedy economy — three words that perfectly crystallize Jack's relationship with Liz (paternal, dismissive, affectionate in its own way). The 'nerd' is doing a lot of work here. Among the episode's most quotable lines.

jokes.text: Rosemary, that was such a rush standing up to Jack like that. And I never would have done it if it weren't for you. / Jack says you're both fired.
jokes.setup: Liz is elated from her confrontation with Jack, celebrating her defiance with Rosemary
jokes.punchline: A page immediately deflates the moment — they're both fired
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke — the immediate deflation of Liz's triumph is a well-timed punchline. The rapid turnaround (Liz barely finishes her victory speech) makes it land well. Slightly predictable but executed efficiently.

jokes.text: Rosemary reacts to being fired with an enthusiastic 'Yes!'
jokes.setup: Both Liz and Rosemary are fired; Liz is clearly devastated
jokes.punchline: Rosemary's jubilant 'Yes!' — she's thrilled to be fired, which reframes everything about her character
jokes.explanation: Single-word reaction that completely recontextualizes Rosemary — she wanted to be fired from the corporate machine. Maximum economy. The rewatch bonus applies because the 'Yes!' becomes funnier knowing where Rosemary lives and how she actually exists outside NBC.

jokes.text: I don't need therapy. I'm just mentally ill.
jokes.setup: Jack suggests Tracy needs therapy to work through his father issues
jokes.punchline: Tracy distinguishes between needing therapy (a weakness) and simply being mentally ill (apparently neutral/factual to him)
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's absolute best lines. The distinction Tracy draws — between needing therapy and being mentally ill — is absurd, logical within his worldview, and perfectly character-integrated. It's the kind of line that sounds like it couldn't be improved by a single word. The delivery implied is flat sincerity, which makes it devastating. Highly quotable, strong rewatch value. Comparable in craft to the anchor examples.

jokes.text: Tracy, what if I told you that the one thing you cannot do is therapy? / You're not my dad! We're doing therapy!
jokes.setup: Tracy refuses therapy; Jack pivots to using Tracy's own psychology against him
jokes.punchline: Tracy immediately adopts the exact pattern Jack diagnosed — defiance as motivation — but now in the direction Jack wants
jokes.explanation: Exceptional payoff to the running gag — Jack weaponizes the 'You're not my dad!' pattern to make Tracy do the right thing, and Tracy falls for it completely. The 'You're not my dad! We're doing therapy!' is a brilliant inversion. Perfect structure, maximum character integration. Among the episode's top moments.

jokes.text: A page-off? What's that? / It's a savage contest. Mixing physical stamina with NBC trivia.
jokes.setup: Donnie proposes a 'page-off' to resolve their dispute
jokes.punchline: The page-off described as 'a savage contest mixing physical stamina with NBC trivia' — treating what is a minor workplace dispute as gladiatorial combat
jokes.explanation: The disproportionate seriousness applied to NBC page trivia as a 'savage contest' is a great piece of institutional absurdism. The show's affection for treating minor hierarchies with epic gravity is well-executed here.

jokes.text: I don't know what kind of corporate mind games he's playing. But if Jack thinks I'm crawling back there... Oh, screw him. / Now that you're free, we can work on something together! Yeah, we can start our own network called Bitch TV!
jokes.setup: Liz and Rosemary are newly fired and riding a wave of freedom
jokes.punchline: Rosemary's immediate pivot to 'Bitch TV' as their new venture — the confidence and specificity is funny
jokes.explanation: The followup beat — 'Or the second idea that we think of' — makes this better. Rosemary's unfiltered enthusiasm for 'Bitch TV' is charming, and Liz's polite hedge acknowledges they probably need another idea. Good character dynamic.

jokes.text: Or the second idea that we think of.
jokes.setup: Rosemary pitches 'Bitch TV' as their new network
jokes.punchline: Liz's diplomatic suggestion that maybe they could also consider the 'second idea' — implying Bitch TV is not it, delivered with polite desperation
jokes.explanation: Six-word diplomatic retreat from 'Bitch TV.' The economy is nearly perfect — 'the second idea that we think of' is wonderfully indirect and very Liz Lemon. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: What neighborhood is this? / Oh, they call it little Chechnya. So gritty and real. More murders per capita than Detroit. Try not to write when you're living here. Is that guy carrying a gun? / Yeah, but don't worry. He's not a cop.
jokes.setup: Rosemary takes Liz to her apartment, which is apparently in a terrible neighborhood
jokes.punchline: 'Little Chechnya' / 'more murders per capita than Detroit' / 'He's not a cop' — each detail escalates the horror Rosemary presents as a feature
jokes.explanation: The escalating horror of Rosemary's neighborhood sold as 'gritty and real' is excellent dark comedy. Each new detail ('more murders per capita than Detroit,' 'he's not a cop') lands because Rosemary presents it all with pride. The 'try not to write when you're living here' is a particularly good implicit joke — the neighborhood is so bad it kills creativity.

jokes.text: I'd like to hop right in and start with some role play. / Like my wife and I do? Cool. You be the maid. I want you to scream.
jokes.setup: The therapist proposes role play as a therapy technique
jokes.punchline: Tracy immediately applies his own marriage's role-play dynamic, assigning the therapist as 'the maid' and demanding screaming
jokes.explanation: Tracy's complete inability to hear 'role play' in any context other than his home life is strong character comedy. The specificity — 'the maid' and 'I want you to scream' — implies a very specific domestic situation without explaining it, which is funnier.

jokes.text: Donaghy, you play the matador.
jokes.setup: Tracy is assigning therapy roles based on his home role-play
jokes.punchline: Jack is assigned 'the matador' — a completely inexplicable role with no connection to anything, which somehow makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: The matador is the joke — purely absurdist, no explanation given or needed. The randomness of 'matador' in a list that includes 'the maid' is the kind of specific-absurdist detail 30 Rock does brilliantly. Jack's implied reaction to being assigned matador duties is the silent laugh.

jokes.text: All I know is he's from funky north Philly. He worked in a Campbell's soup factory. And he had a droopy lip due to an unattended root canal. / I think I can do this.
jokes.setup: The therapist asks where Tracy's father is from so Jack can roleplay him
jokes.punchline: The three details Tracy knows about his father — 'funky north Philly,' Campbell's soup factory, droopy lip from neglected dental work — are hilariously specific and sad. Jack's 'I think I can do this' implies he can do a droopy-lipped Campbell's worker.
jokes.explanation: The three details about Tracy's father are perfectly calibrated — each one sadder and more specific than the last. 'Funky north Philly' is vague but evocative; 'Campbell's soup factory' is achingly specific; 'droopy lip due to an unattended root canal' is a devastating poverty detail delivered as comedy. Jack's confidence that he can perform this is the payoff. Strong thematic and comedic work.

jokes.text: The therapy roleplay scene spirals into Jack playing multiple characters (Tracy's dad, his mom, a white stepfather, a Latina neighbor Mrs. Rodriguez) with increasingly absurd results
jokes.setup: Jack has agreed to roleplay Tracy's estranged father
jokes.punchline: The scene escalates into a full domestic drama with Jack playing multiple characters — including 'Mrs. Rodriguez' screaming from offstage — until it becomes pure absurdist chaos
jokes.explanation: The therapy scene as a whole is a masterpiece of escalating absurdism — Jack playing a Philly factory worker, then a welfare-receiving mother, then a white stepfather concerned about soup manners, then 'Mrs. Rodriguez' is both structurally brilliant and a showcase for Baldwin's range. High rewatch bonus because each viewing reveals more comic layers.

jokes.text: Hey, dummy! / I'm mad at you too. Why you gotta act out that way? / That's not exactly what I had in... / 'Cause you left me, dad! / I was young and confused and your moms didn't want me around no more. Now, pass me them damn collard greens!
jokes.setup: Jack attempts a therapeutic roleplay as Tracy's father per the therapist's guidance
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately abandons therapeutic aims and becomes genuinely combative as 'Tracy's dad' — 'Hey, dummy!' and demanding collard greens mid-argument
jokes.explanation: Jack throwing himself into the role — complete with 'Hey, dummy!' and the collard greens demand — is one of the episode's best sequences. The therapist's futile interjections ('That's not exactly what I had in...') are the perfect straight-man beat. The WASP millionaire Jack Donaghy performing 'funky north Philly Campbell's soup worker' is inherently funny and escalates beautifully.

jokes.text: Whoa, no need to resort to ugly stereotypes.
jokes.setup: Jack does a perfect patrician white character for Tracy's stepfather
jokes.punchline: The therapist — who has been watching Jack and Liz do racial and class caricatures for several minutes — suddenly objects to the white stereotype
jokes.explanation: The irony of the therapist only objecting to the white stereotype (after allowing Black and Hispanic caricatures) is a sharp satirical beat about which stereotypes trigger discomfort. Well-timed but slightly underplayed.

jokes.text: Lady, just because I'm an ignorant black man. And you paid me a nickel to bust up your chifforobe, doesn't give you the right to call me ridiculous just 'cause I'm proud of my son.
jokes.setup: The roleplay has become a sprawling neighborhood drama
jokes.punchline: Jack's monologue invokes To Kill a Mockingbird (chifforobe is a direct reference to Tom Robinson's scene) while ostensibly playing a north Philly working man — the literary reference is both absurd and reveals Jack's patrician education leaking through the character
jokes.explanation: Exceptional layered joke — Jack the WASP patrician is so committed to playing an 'ignorant black man' that he accidentally invokes a specific scene from To Kill a Mockingbird (Tom Robinson's testimony about busting up a chifforobe). The literary slip reveals Jack's prep school background even when he's trying to do otherwise. Strong originality, excellent character integration for Jack specifically.

jokes.text: They got me. The honkeys shot me. / No, dad! Don't die! I love you, dad! / I don't wanna dog fight no more!
jokes.setup: The roleplay reaches a climax with Tracy's 'dad' being shot
jokes.punchline: Tracy's breakthrough — his emotional catharsis about his father connects directly to his resolution about dog fighting, delivered at peak emotional intensity
jokes.explanation: The payoff to multiple plot threads simultaneously — the father issues, the dog fighting subplot, and the therapy roleplay — delivered at maximum emotional pitch. The juxtaposition of genuine emotional release ('I love you, dad!') with 'I don't wanna dog fight no more!' is the comedic structure working at its best.

jokes.text: Thank you for showing me there really is love in my family after all. And I need to stay the hell away from them.
jokes.setup: Tracy has an apparent emotional breakthrough about his family
jokes.punchline: The lesson Tracy draws is the opposite of the intended therapeutic outcome — love them AND stay away from them
jokes.explanation: A perfect one-two comedy structure — the first half sounds like a genuine breakthrough, the second half inverts it into a very Tracy Jordan conclusion. 'I need to stay the hell away from them' as a lesson about the importance of family is both funny and somehow emotionally resonant. Highly quotable, excellent character integration.

jokes.text: You know, it's too bad you didn't know Howard Cosell when you were growing up. 'Cause I had that one in my pocket the whole time.
jokes.setup: The therapy session resolves; Jack reflects
jokes.punchline: Jack's casual admission that he had a Howard Cosell impression ready to use as another 'fake dad' character but didn't get to deploy it
jokes.explanation: This joke rewards attention — Jack has been doing character work the whole scene and is now almost wistful about a missed opportunity to use his Howard Cosell impression. The 'I had that one in my pocket' implies he was waiting for an opening. Excellent character specific humor — only Jack Donaghy would have a prepared Cosell impression for therapy emergencies.

jokes.text: Women in their 50s join the army and get laid by a bunch of grateful 18 year olds. I predict opening weekend, a million dollars.
jokes.setup: Liz and Rosemary are writing their screenplay together
jokes.punchline: Rosemary's movie pitch is brazenly wish-fulfillment, delivered with total confidence — and the $1M opening weekend prediction is deliberately modest as a punchline
jokes.explanation: The screenplay pitch captures Rosemary's unself-conscious wish-fulfillment perfectly. 'A million dollars' as a bold opening weekend prediction (an extremely modest sum for a film) is the kind of specific detail that lands — she's both ambitious and completely out of touch.

jokes.text: Rosemary: 'I predict opening weekend, a million dollars.'
jokes.setup: Rosemary has pitched her army sex fantasy screenplay
jokes.punchline: Her projected opening weekend gross is $1 million — a comically small number that reveals her complete disconnection from the modern film industry
jokes.explanation: Efficiently lands another Rosemary-is-out-of-touch joke. In 2007, a $1 million opening weekend was a catastrophic flop; she says it with the confidence of someone who last tracked box office in 1974. The specificity of 'a million dollars' (not 'ten million' or 'a hundred million') is perfect.

jokes.text: Have you been drinking wine all day? / Oh, it's heart healthy. / All day? / Oh, come on, Liz. It's the 90s!
jokes.setup: Liz notices Rosemary has been drinking
jokes.punchline: Rosemary's time disorientation — defending wine with a 90s reference, apparently unaware it's no longer the 90s — reveals the depth of her detachment from reality
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character beats. 'Oh, come on, Liz. It's the 90s!' delivered sincerely is a devastating revelation — Rosemary is living a decade behind in her own head. This crystallizes her character and Liz's growing horror at the future she's looking at. Highly quotable, strong character integration.

jokes.text: Did an F train just go by your window? / I know that look. Don't even think about jumping for that train.
jokes.setup: A subway train apparently passes directly by Rosemary's window
jokes.punchline: Rosemary — experienced with desperate apartment visitors — immediately recognizes the escape impulse and cuts it off
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag inferred from dialogue — a subway train passing by the window at eye level implies a terrifying apartment, and Rosemary's experienced knowledge that visitors want to leap onto trains is both funny and slightly tragic. The economy is strong.

jokes.text: You pick up guys that are smart and funny. And they leave you for someone less complicated. You're never gonna get married, Liz. You're married to your job. / Oh my god. I lost my job.
jokes.setup: Rosemary tells Liz they're the same — drawing unflattering parallels
jokes.punchline: Rosemary's devastating 'you're married to your job' lands simultaneously with Liz realizing she no longer has the job
jokes.explanation: The comedic irony of 'you're married to your job' landing at the exact moment Liz remembers she lost the job is elegantly structured. Rosemary's unintentional cruelty (she forgot Liz got fired) is funnier because it's not intentional. Good callback, strong character resonance.

jokes.text: You get up in the morning and smoke weed... / No, I don't. / You obsess about the Jamaican man across the hall. / Oh, my god. I lost my job.
jokes.setup: Rosemary continues cataloguing how Liz is just like her
jokes.punchline: Liz keeps short-circuiting back to 'Oh my god, I lost my job' instead of engaging with the comparisons, and her denial of smoking weed vs her non-denial about the Jamaican man implies the Jamaican man detail is true
jokes.explanation: Good structural use of a running beat — Liz's horror at job loss keeps resurfacing. The structural joke is that she only denies the weed (not the Jamaican man), implying the man is real. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I sat around while my junk went bad. All for you. I didn't have any kids. You're my kid! You're my kid that never calls!
jokes.setup: Rosemary escalates her claims on Liz's identity and loyalty
jokes.punchline: 'I sat around while my junk went bad' is the specific, horrifying, funny detail in an escalating guilt trip
jokes.explanation: The escalating guilt trip builds to the absurd and honest 'my junk went bad' — a direct and funny way to describe biological clock sacrifice. The pivot to 'You're my kid that never calls' is a strong comedic closer to the guilt sequence.

jokes.text: Help me, Liz Lemon! You're my only hope!
jokes.setup: Rosemary is desperately trying to keep Liz from leaving
jokes.punchline: A Star Wars reference ('Help me, Obi-Wan Kenobi!') applied to Liz — the absurdity of framing Liz as a messiah figure after establishing her as a 'follower' is the joke
jokes.explanation: A Star Wars reference that works okay — using Liz's full name in the Obi-Wan slot is the specific detail that saves it from being too easy. Not 30 Rock's most original moment but functional.

jokes.text: Okay, which NBC series spun off, among others, Cosby, Miami Vice, Cheers, and Highway to Heaven? / Supercomputer!
jokes.setup: The page-off trivia question is posed
jokes.punchline: 'Supercomputer!' — Ms. Moroney answers with the name of the 1975-1975 show from earlier, which is clearly not the correct answer but allows the callback to land
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'Supercomputer' — the show that ran from 1975 to 1975 — as the answer to a trivia question about a landmark NBC series is a neat structural joke. The rewatch bonus applies for catching that she's answering with the obscure series from Donnie's office.

jokes.text: Hey! What the hell is going on down here? The phones are ringing off the hook, there's no one seating the Conan audience! Get back to work, you morons!
jokes.setup: The page-off has apparently drawn a crowd and paralyzed NBC operations
jokes.punchline: Pete's practical outrage at the NBC operational chaos (Conan's audience unattended!) is the straight-man deflation of the absurd page-off drama
jokes.explanation: Pete's practical authority is a good straight-man beat. The specific detail 'no one seating the Conan audience' grounds the absurdity of the page-off in actual NBC logistics, which is the right move for a workplace comedy. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: This isn't over between us, Moroney. You're in it now.
jokes.setup: Pete forces Donnie to give Kenneth a new jacket without the page-off
jokes.punchline: Donnie's theatrical villain sign-off — treating a jacket dispute as a blood feud
jokes.explanation: Standard villain-signing-off beat. Functional escalation of Donnie's antagonism but not particularly original. The mismatch between the threat level and the actual stakes (a jacket) is the joke.

jokes.text: It's finally over, Ms. Moroney. / Yes. / And it's hard to even remember how it all began. [beat] / You burnt my jacket.
jokes.setup: Kenneth and Ms. Moroney reflect on their ordeal in the manner of epic survivors
jokes.punchline: The punchline is Ms. Moroney's flat 'You burnt my jacket' — deflating the epic framing by immediately remembering the mundane origin
jokes.explanation: The structural joke here is elegant — the epic battle callback deflated by the simplest possible explanation ('You burnt my jacket'), delivered with a perfect beat before it. The beat between 'how it all began' and the matter-of-fact answer is the comedy. Strong callback, excellent economy.

jokes.text: All right, I need my job back. But this is not crawling, this is proud begging, like those kids that dance on the subway.
jokes.setup: Liz returns to Jack's office to ask for her job back
jokes.punchline: The distinction between 'crawling' and 'proud begging' — with the subway dancers as the reference point for dignified desperation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The distinction between 'crawling' and 'proud begging' is a perfectly observed piece of psychological self-deception, and the subway dancers as the emblem of dignified desperation is a brilliant, specific, New York-native analogy. Extremely quotable, excellent character integration — only Liz would construct this self-justification.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Never go with a hippie to a second location.'
jokes.setup: Liz recounts her traumatic visit to Rosemary's apartment — the bathroom situation, the depressing future vision
jokes.punchline: Jack distills the entire lesson into a single epigram: 'Never go with a hippie to a second location' — delivered as timeless wisdom
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke and a 30 Rock all-timer. This is the calibration anchor provided in the brief, and it deserves its score. The joke works as a riff on the 'never go to a second location' safety rule, applied with perfect specificity to 'hippie.' It's delivered by Jack as genuine life wisdom, which is both funny in itself (his patrician worldview) and genuinely useful as advice. Maximum economy — eight words that couldn't be improved. Highly quotable, culturally durable, perfectly placed as the episode's turning-point punchline.

jokes.text: Never go with a hippie to a second location.
jokes.setup: Liz describes her experience at Rosemary's terrible apartment
jokes.punchline: The distilled wisdom: never follow a hippie to their place — delivered as a maxim, based on lived experience
jokes.explanation: The single best joke in the episode and one of the all-time great 30 Rock one-liners. It earns 9+ by meeting the anchor criteria: comparable to 'Never go with a hippie to a second location' IS the anchor example cited in the scoring guide, and it appears verbatim in this transcript. Sharp, unexpected, highly quotable, perfect economy. The joke works as genuine practical wisdom, absurdist comedy, and character comedy simultaneously. Liz has synthesized her entire experience into one portable truth.

jokes.text: I have to do that thing that rich people do where they turn money into more money. Can you teach me how to do that? / With my eyes closed.
jokes.setup: Liz explains she needs to learn about investing
jokes.punchline: 'That thing that rich people do where they turn money into more money' — Liz's earnest description of investing as if it's alchemy — and Jack's confident 'With my eyes closed'
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the opening financial ignorance joke. Liz's description of investing as 'the thing rich people do where they turn money into more money' is perfectly observed naïveté, and Jack's 'with my eyes closed' is the right level of patrician confidence.

jokes.text: Oh, and by the way, I want to send Rosemary $400 a month for... forever. / You should, that woman is unemployable.
jokes.setup: Liz wants to send Rosemary financial support
jokes.punchline: Jack's endorsement — 'You should, that woman is unemployable' — validates the charity while being maximally unkind about Rosemary
jokes.explanation: Jack's casual 'unemployable' as a benediction rather than a criticism is great character work — he means it practically, not cruelly. The matter-of-fact tone elevates what could be a mean joke into something funnier.

jokes.text: Rosemary says that women become obsolete in this business when there's no one left that wants to see them naked. / You make enough money, you can pay people to look at you naked.
jokes.setup: Liz quotes Rosemary's bleak wisdom about women in entertainment
jokes.punchline: Jack's solution — wealth makes nakedness voluntary and commercially available — is both horrifying and completely in-character
jokes.explanation: A two-part joke where both halves land. Rosemary's line about women becoming obsolete is genuinely dark and sharp Hollywood commentary. Jack's solution ('pay people to look at you naked') is a perfect Donaghy response — transactional, amoral, and oddly optimistic. Strong character integration for both.

jokes.text: Oh, and by the way, GE has a problem with the dog penis sketch. / I'll change it. [beat] / Hey, what about cat penises?
jokes.setup: Jack drops a final note as Liz is leaving
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately agrees, then almost immediately offers a workaround — cat penises — as if this is a reasonable creative solution
jokes.explanation: A perfect episode closer. The callback to the dog penis sketch pays off with Liz's sincere solution — cat penises — delivered after a beat that implies she thought hard about it. It's the final word on the episode's theme: Liz claims creative integrity but will always find a way to work within the system. Excellent economy, strong character integration, very quotable tag.

tmdb_overview: Liz meets her longtime idol, Rosemary Howard, and invites her to be a guest writer on "TGS with Tracy Jordan". However, Rosemary's ideas turn out to be too much for the show, prompting Jack to pressure Liz into firing her. Meanwhile, Jack takes Tracy to a therapist to explain to him why he must do the opposite of what he is told, and Jenna ruins Kenneth's page jacket, causing him to compete in a page-off to keep his job.
insight: Subversive character comedy sustains 81-point episode despite sparse standout moments.
